html:
The Nile is the great river of north-east Africa, flowing north into the Mediterranean. At between about 6,650 and 7,100 kilometres, depending on how it is measured, it is often called the longest river in the world.

It has two main branches. The White Nile flows from Lake Victoria through Uganda and South Sudan. The Blue Nile comes down from the highlands of Ethiopia and brings most of the water and, in the past, the summer flood. The two meet at Khartoum in Sudan. Below there the river crosses the desert in a narrow green strip, broken by six cataracts, rocky rapids.

For thousands of years the yearly flood laid fresh silt on the fields of Egypt. It fed the pharaohs' state and later fed Rome, and the river was Egypt's main road. Upstream, Nubia had its own kingdoms along the river, from Kerma, with its huge mud-brick Western Deffufa, to Napata and Meroë of Kush.

European explorers spent much of the 1800s searching for its sources; David Livingstone died looking for them. In the 1900s the river was tamed. The Aswan High Dam, finished in 1970, ended the flood and made electricity, and Egypt drew water from Lake Nasser for the Toshka project. Upstream, Ethiopia's Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam on the Blue Nile has caused a long quarrel with Egypt and Sudan over the river's water.
